# About the author

This demo knowledge base is built and maintained independently.

My name is José Manuel Salgado Arriaga, and I am based in Mexico. I hold a bachelor’s degree in oceanography from [FCM UABC](http://fcm.ens.uabc.mx/) and a master’s degree in education from [IIDE UABC](https://iide.ens.uabc.mx/).

For a few years, I worked as a creative writer, producing articles such as [these on Career Karma](https://careerkarma.com/blog/author/jose/). In 2022, at a client's request, I pivoted into software documentation, helping Publicis Groupe write version 2 of the user guide for its internal project management software (rOar PPM). Realizing the importance of video in illustrating software functionality, I also became an advanced, certified user of [Camtasia](https://www.techsmith.com/camtasia/).

After completing self-guided training and certifications in data science, I joined AnyTrack as a technical writer, client success specialist, and knowledge base manager. From 2023 to 2025, I authored or coauthored many of the articles found in the [AnyTrack Knowledge Base](https://readme.anytrack.io/docs).

Since 2025, I have worked as an independent freelance contractor for [XLeap](https://www.xleap.net/), helping produce a series of software explainer videos. In late 2026, I developed this demo knowledge base site for portfolio purposes, incorporating industry best practices and standards while relying exclusively on free, open-source technologies that ensure full data sovereignty.

## Contact & Hire

* **Email:** hola@josemanuelsalgado.com

* **Upwork:** Hire me as a technical writer or knowledge base manager via my [Upwork Profile](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/~018d3a31f0feb078ff), where I have billed over 880 hours, earned $20K+ in total revenue, and maintained a 100% Job Success score.

content:

sidebar_position: 2

# About this demo

This demo aims at showcasing:
  1. How the technologies used in it work. 
  2. My epistemological approach to SaaS documentation.
  3. The advantages of using a live Knowledge Base as opposed to a PDF file.
 

## Production pipeline (processes) 

### Step 1. Write an article in markdown

The content is written in [Markdown](https://www.markdownguide.org/getting-started/) (a markup language like HTML but simpler, lighter, and more readable, it is the industry standard for documentation).
So this is how it looks like as I am writting this article using Visual Studio Code:

![Writing this article in VSC](./img/writing.png)

### Step 2. Run Build on terminal and preview changes locally (docusaurus engine)

Docusausus is a free, open-source static site engine contributed by Meta to the open source community. 
I download and install docusaurus on my computer.
Docusaurus is React based, so it uses javascript and React to render the content into a lightweight, fast, and responsive website.

once the content is written in markdown I run Docusaurus:

![Building the static site](./img/build.png)

### Step 3. Push changes to GitHub

I have git and github (version control) on my computer so I have added the project folder to a git repository and pushed it to my github account.
I comment each commit in case it is necessary to roll back the specific changes in this commit.

![Committing and commenting changes pushed to Github](./img/github.png)

### Step 4. Vercel deployment server updates automatically to new release.

So finally I used Vercel to deploy the website. Vercel is a cloud platform for static sites and serverless functions that fits perfectly with Docusaurus. 
It is free for personal projects and it is very easy to use. However, the website can also be deployed on any other free or paid hosting service that supports static websites (for example an azure web app).

![Vercel updates deployment](./img/vercel.png)


## My Epistemological Approach

While documenting every single feature of a software product as if it were a machine dashboard is sometimes an acceptable approach, modern software documentation places an increasing emphasis on real-life scenarios—where users visit the documentation seeking answers to specific problems. Once users arrive, we use whatever artifacts are necessary to ensure they reach full understanding. This often involves a dynamic combination of text, images, videos, diagrams, examples, interactive simulations, and related articles. If needed, an LLM chatbot component can be integrated to allow further exploration via natural language. As a failsafe, the documentation should always provide a direct option to contact support.

## Architecture

Using the industry standards of knowledge base design (eg. the Google  documetation style guide https://developers.google.com/style), same for microsoft, etc.
we see that the left side navigation bar is a great way to structure sections and then its subsections.




## Disclaimers

### Not an official xleap KB 
This demo site is a proof of concept and not an official channel from XLeap Gmbh, for official channels please visit [https://www.xleap.net/](https://www.xleap.net/)

### Generative AI used in this demo

The texts in this KB were written by [myself](https://x-leap-docs-demo.vercel.app/docs/about/about%20the%20author). Generative AI (Gemini, free tier) was used to edit many sections
of this KB, mainly to make the sentences more succint, further editorial review is obviously needed and will be gradually implemented .

Manual adjustments to the settings of the knowledge base were first consulted with Copilot (gpt6-luna, free tier).


### Open source project

This project and its files, contained in its [github repo](https://github.com/jose-salgado81/demo-knowledge-base) uses free, [open-source](https://opensource.org/osd) technologies to ensure 
independence from subscription services and to prevent sudden changes in usability imposed from third parties. The repository is open to the public so every file
can be inspected, or even cloned. For this, no authorization is required.

title: about/Why Knowlege Base
content:
--- sidebar_position: 1 --- # Why a Knowledge Base? You might be wondering why would you want a knowledge base (KB), when the documentation of your software can be contained in a standard PDF file. In this article you will learn why a knowledge base is a superior approach to software documentation. If you need further persuasion, visit this [Atlassian article](https://www.atlassian.com/itsm/knowledge-management/what-is-a-knowledge-base). ## 1. Continuous Updates and Version Control In a Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment workflow, documentation must evolve alongside your code to prevent mismatches. The Docs-as-Code approach manages your KB in a Git repository like GitHub, allowing team members to draft and test updates in separate branches before merging them into production. This setup provides complete version control, tracking history and comments so you can easily audit changes or roll back versions. Ultimately, treating documentation as code ensures users always access accurate, up-to-date information that matches your latest software releases. ![Git Comment](./img/git%20comment.png) ## 2. Display Adaptiveness and Dark Theme Since the KB renders on the browser as a webpage, the display is adaptive and displays according to the device screen and the browser preferences. It is easy to switch between dark and light themes. ![Switch to activate the dark theme of the knowledge base](./img/dark.png) ## 3. Embedded Media Markdown allows to embed different types of media such as images and videos. The following is an animaged gif image: ![This is an animated gif image showing project media files](./img/animated.gif) To learn about the possibilities for video in the Knowledge Base, visit the [video library section](/docs/videolibrary/Video%20Library). ## 4. LLMs Ready Large Language Models (LLMs) learn about software by processing websites and user manuals. While they can learn from various file types, they prefer Markdown language, since it is machine-readable and explicitly structures knowledge hierarchy and mark up. Key advantages of Markdown for LLMs: - Image Context: Models can read alt tags to reference images even if they aren't multimodal. - LLM-Specific Instructions: Allows embedding notes and guidance directly for model interpretation. - Metadata Support: Easily incorporates SEO tags and markers for crawlers and indexers. Learn more at: [Why Markdown is the Best Format for LLMs](https://medium.com/@wetrocloud/why-markdown-is-the-best-format-for-llms-aa0514a409a7) ## 5. Artifacts In a knowledge base that uses markdown it is possible to embed dynamic artifacts, for example: ### 5.1 Accordions
Click here to expand and read more This is the hidden content inside the accordion. You can put text, bullet points, or even images here: - Item one - Item two
### 5.2 Callouts :::note This is a standard note callout to highlight important information. ::: :::tip Here is a helpful tip or best practice you can share with users. ::: :::info Use an info callout for general supplementary details. ::: :::warning Be careful! This warns the user about a potential pitfall or breaking change. ::: :::danger Critical warning! Use this for dangerous actions or destructive steps. ::: ### 5.3 Diagrams The KB allows to use code (mermaid syntax) to create diagrams. Use diagrams to illustrate processes or decision-making. Since the diagrams are based on code and not images, they are very light even if they hold a lot of detail and they can be understood by both humans and llms. Example: ```mermaid graph TD A[Start: After entering brainstorm ideas] --> B{Are the brainstorm ideas diverse?} B -->|Yes| C[Categorize in Folders] B -->|No| D[Proceed to Ratings] D --> A ``` To learn more about the possibilities of mermaid diagrams, visit the [Diagrams section](/docs/diagrams/mermaid.mdx) ### 5.4 Code Blocks If you need to communicate code that can be easily copy and pasted ```javascript function greetUser(name) { console.log("Hello, " + name + "!"); } greetUser("Developer"); ``` ### 5.5 HTML and JS ready This knowledge base uses [MDX](https://mdxjs.com/docs/what-is-mdx/), which allows you to mix Markdown, raw HTML, and JavaScript right inside the article. #### A . Standard HTML Styling You can use standard HTML tags with inline styles:

HTML Box: This element is written using raw HTML and CSS directly inside the Markdown file.

#### B. Interactive JavaScript / Scripts You can also attach event handlers and JavaScript functionality using JSX syntax: ## 6. LLM Assistant Ready The latest release of Chrome (and many other browsers) now includes an LLM assistant that helps users "talk" with the webpage. Because this website is built as a static HTML site derived from Markdown, it renders clean, semantic HTML and structure (such as clear heading hierarchies and alt tags) that makes it exceptionally effective for browser-based LLM assistants to understand the content. ![Chrome browser showing the Gemini assistant tab explaining the KB article](./img/gemini.png) ## 7. Search and Share It is easy to integrate local search in the KB using React components. You can test it now, it quickly searches across all articles in the knowledge base: ![copy a link that points to specific sections'](./img/local.png) In addition to local search functionality, Google will index the KB considering the knowledge hierarchy as established in the sitemap.xml file that is automatically generated by docusaurus on every KB build run . [View the sitemap](https://x-leap-docs-demo.vercel.app/sitemap.xml) To share knowledge, instead of sharing a link to the KB, share a link to a specific section in a specific article. To do this, simply copy the anchor link found at the end of each heading. ![copy a link that points to specific sections'](./img/share.png) ## 8. Analytics It is possible to know which are the most reviewed articles and sections of the documentation. In the case of this knowledge base I have placed a Google Analytics Tag , so on my GA4 dashboard I can see which audiences are visiting, what they are reading and for how long. ![GA4 dashboard with stats about visitors to the knowledge base](./img/ga4.png) Also you can get instant feedback from the user's experience with the "Was this useful" widget, so you can implement a natural selection evolution approach to the curation of the knowledge base. Find the vote option at the bottom of the article ![was this page useful](./img/vote.png) ## 9. Data Sovereignty This KB relies entirely on open-source technologies, meaning no third party controls its display or vendor-locks your content. Unlike commercial platforms such as **[Readme](https://readme.io)** and **[GitBook](https://www.gitbook.com)**—which force you to depend on proprietary hosting and tooling—the system generating this KB runs locally on your computer. You retain complete ownership and can migrate your hosting provider or deploy to any cloud compute or container platform at any time. ## 11 . Batch edits Since the documentation is code, you can edit it using code tools like Find and Replace. In the following image I'm replacing the word 'demo' with 'trial' across all articles in the knowledge base ![Using Find and Replace in Visual Studio Code to replace 'demo' with 'trial'](./img/find.png) ## 12. Navigation and knowledge hierarchy The left sidebar maps all sections and articles for easy navigation, while the right-side floating table of contents helps you track your place and jump between sections quickly. This follows the latest trends in best documentation practices. ## 13. Be the leading source of truth for your software In a world where LLMs can be used to render stories that cater to the interests of whoever is using them, an official knowledge base is perhaps the best way to maintain editorial control over how your product is explained to the world. Develop arguments that support your claims so that users understand not only how the software functions, but also the design principles behind it. A knowledge base can be much more than a user's manual—it can articulate why people should use your software, effectively serving as a platform that advances your value proposition. For example, in the case of XLeap, the KB can be the place where people learn why anonymity when sharing ideas during a collaborative session leads to better meeting outcomes. ## 14. Reduce customer support ticket volume First touch point in your customer service/client success/training pipeline. To reduce the volume of support tickets, have your users first consult the Knowledge Base, and after using the search engine (or a support chatbot) they will check an article only if the article/chatbot was unable to be useful route the user to a ticket system for personal support. Then you are able to know which articles they read and determine why is it that the article wasn't enough.

title: diagrams/mermaid
content:
--- sidebar_position: 2 --- # Mermaid Diagrams ## Overview Mermaid is an open source JavaScript-based diagramming syntax that is becoming the standard in the software documentation industry. Mermaid lets you describe diagrams as simple text and render them into visual flowcharts or sequence diagrams without image files, right in the browser. Large Language Models (LLMs) can read the plain-text syntax and understand the diagram, even if the LLM doesn't include an image processing component. So it is very economical for llms to process and learn from Mermaid diagrams. To learn more about Mermaid diagrams visit [this site](https://mermaid.ai/open-source/intro/index.html). Mermaid diagrams are useful when you want to explain a process or architecture directly inside your documentation. ### Example 1: Sequence Diagram (How a bill becomes law in the USA) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Sponsor as Bill sponsor participant Committee as Congressional committee participant House as House of Representatives participant Senate as Senate participant President as President Sponsor->>Committee: Introduce bill Committee->>House: Report bill for vote House->>Senate: Pass amended bill Senate-->>House: Return with changes House->>President: Send final bill President-->>Sponsor: Sign into law or veto ``` If you are curious about the code used to render the previous diagram, it is the following: ```javascript mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Sponsor as Bill sponsor participant Committee as Congressional committee participant House as House of Representatives participant Senate as Senate participant President as President Sponsor->>Committee: Introduce bill Committee->>House: Report bill for vote House->>Senate: Pass amended bill Senate-->>House: Return with changes House->>President: Send final bill President-->>Sponsor: Sign into law or veto ``` ### Example 2: Another Sequence Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Alice participant Bob Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you? loop HealthCheck John->>John: Fight against hypochondria end Note right of John: Rational thoughts
prevail! John-->>Alice: Great! John->>Bob: How about you? Bob-->>John: Jolly good! ```

title: invitationdialogue/Login Requirements
content: --- sidebar_position: 1 --- *This is an example of how I would draft an article for the XLeap knowledge base.* In this article you will learn how to set login requirements for your session according to your session objectives. There are four login requirement options available to the host 1. [None](#none). Use this option to allow anyone with the link to join the session 2. Name 3. [Name and Email](#name-and-email).Name and Email. This is the standard setting 4. [Username and password](#username-and-password). Use this option to ensure only invited individuals can join your session. ## None This option could rather be useful for informal quick meetings :::danger[Warning] With this option, anyone with the link can join the session, if this goes beyond the scope of your privacy please select a different option. ::: ## Name and Email Name and email allows you to keep it simple and have great awareness of who will be able to join. ## Username and Password Setting username and password as a login requirement allows you select specific invitees from a user database or import them from an Excel file. This is perhaps the most restrictive login requirement option. ### Step by step guide 1. Within the session, click the invitation dialogue button on the toolbar ![User Pass Description](./img/selectinvite.png) 2. On **Login requirements**, click the edit option 3. Select **Username and password** 4. If you are ready to apoint your invitees, click **List of invited users** ![User Pass Description](./img/usernameandpassword.png) This will bring the List of Invitees dialogue from which you can choose from two options, [From user database](#from-user-database) and [Import list of invited users](#import-list-of-invitees) ![User Pass Description](./img/listof.png) ### From user database Selecting to add from user database will allow you to filter and find specific individuals from the database. ![User Pass Description](./img/inv.gif) contact center admin for changes to this database, note that you can add new users by clicking on Add User ![User Pass Description](./img/add.png) ### Import list of invitees This option allows you to import from an Excel file #### This is an H4 level This is **bold**, this is _italic_ ## This is an orderly list: 1. Item 1 2. Item 1 3. Item 1 4. Item 4 ## This is an unorderly list: - Item 1 - Item 2 - Item 3 - Item 4 :::tip[Good to know] Participants can contribute their ideas later ::: :::danger[Warning] Emptying the trash bin will permently delete all the items. :::

title: videolibrary/Video Library
content:
--- sidebar_position: 2 --- # Video Library This section showcases the video capabilities of this Knowledge Base (KB). Ideally, explainer videos should be embedded directly within the context of their corresponding KB articles. ## YouTube videos Example of a YouTube video embedded in the article (position and size can be adjusted):
## Video Files All modern browsers have an integrated media player, allowing visitors to play MP4, WebM, and other video files directly within the article. Unlike YouTube videos, there are no advertisements or Calls-to-Action (CTAs) prompting users to leave the KB. It is also possible to preset the media player controls. In the following example, the mp4 video is preset to mute, displayed at 50% width, and centered on the page.
## Interactive Cards Sometimes, during a video, you may want to point viewers to ancillary videos or articles. For example, if a video covers Topic B, you might want to recommend watching a video about Topic A first. In the following example, a custom card is configured to appear at the 9-second mark and disappear at the 18-second mark. Every aspect of the card's appearance and timing can be customized. In this example, rather than linking to another video, this card directs you to a specific section within a Knowledge Base article. ## Animated GIF Sometimes you just need an animated gif to illustrate your point. For example, to show how to reveal the **Change nickname AI** option: ![Reveal change AI name option](./img/changename.gif) Sometimes a plain image with steps can be more efficient: To change the AI nickname in the BS workspace, navigate to **Workspace settings** then this (1), then that (2). Finally do (3). ![Steps to change AI nickname](./img/steps.png)
